lines.en: Excuse me. Thirty days in a cave. One million dollars. Interested?
Ha. Sure. What's the catch?
No phone. No light. Nothing but what you're wearing. If you want out, ring the bell. But then you get nothing.
A million dollars? Okay. Okay, deal, I'm in, I just need to—
You wake up in a darkness so complete, it doesn't feel like darkness. It feels like you've gone blind.
Hello? ...Hello?!
Wave your hand in front of your face. Nothing. Your eyes will never adjust. There's nothing for them to adjust to.
Problem number one: you don't know where the ceiling is.
Ow! Okay. Ceiling. Low ceiling. Got it.
So you crawl. And your hand finds a rope, hanging from somewhere far above. When you pull it, a bell rings. The way out. And the end of the million.
Somewhere below you, the deepest cave on Earth goes down for more than two kilometers.
Problem two: the cold. Caves keep the same temperature all year round. Down here, that means about ten degrees. Every day. Every night.
Problem three: the silence. It's so quiet, you start hearing your own heartbeat. Then a ringing that won't stop.
Problem four: direction. In total darkness, nobody walks in a straight line. Ten minutes from where you woke up, you're completely lost.
Problem five: water. You follow the sound of dripping, slip in the mud twice, and lick a wet rock like an animal.
Is that... water? Please be water.
It is. An underground stream, so cold it hurts your teeth. And then the cave answers back.
What was that? What was— AAAH!
Bats. Thousands of them. Leaving for the night you can't see. And problem six, which is just getting started: you're starving.
Day three. Something in the dark is glowing.
A rotten log, washed in by the stream, covered in mushrooms that make their own light. People used to call it foxfire.
Light. LIGHT! Oh, I love you. I love you, little mushroom.
It's barely enough to see your hands. But for the first time, you see where you are. And where you are is enormous.
Problem seven: time. There's no sunrise down here. You sleep, wake up, and have no idea if it was two hours or twenty.
In 1962, a French scientist named Michel Siffre lived two months in a cave without a clock. When they came to get him, he was sure he still had almost a month left.
So you scratch a mark on the wall every time you wake up. And then problem eight lands on your face.
Get off! Get off my face!
A cave cricket. Pale, long legs, very crunchy. Which is a terrible thing to know about something you're about to eat.
It's fine. It's fine. It's... crunchy. It's fine.
Crickets aren't enough. But the stream is full of fish. White, blind fish that have never seen light in a million years.
Problem nine: they're fast. You miss. You miss again. You fall in.
Then you take off your hoodie and stretch it between two rocks like a net. And wait.
Got you! ...I'm so sorry. You're breakfast.
Problem ten: the rocks in the stream are sharp as broken glass. You slice your palm open, tear a strip off your T-shirt, rinse it in the stream, and hope.
Ow, ow, ow. That's fine. That's totally fine.
Problem eleven: nothing dries. The air down here is almost one hundred percent humid. Your hoodie stays wet. You stay wet. And wet plus cold is how people die in caves.
So you follow the air. Higher up, there's a small dry chamber, a little warmer than the rest. Your first bedroom.
Problem twelve: your brain. Starved of light, it starts making its own. Colors. Faces. Whispers. It even has a name: the prisoner's cinema.
Who's there? ...Nobody's there. Nobody's there.
Day eight. You find a backpack. Somebody was here before you.
A tin cup. A pencil. And a diary. Day one: easy money. Day five: the voices. Day nine: I can't anymore. Ringing the bell.
Day nine. You stand at the rope for a long time.
Not today.
Day ten. Problem thirteen: the mushrooms are fading. You need real light.
The walls here are limestone, and limestone hides flint. Strike flint against the shiny golden rock in the stream, pyrite, and you get sparks. That's how people made fire ten thousand years ago.
Come on. Come on. Come ON! ...Fire. I made FIRE!
Problem fourteen, about four seconds later: smoke. In a closed cave, smoke has nowhere to go. Except into you.
So you move the fire to where the air flows, and the cave pulls the smoke up through a crack like a chimney.
Then, the real upgrade. Fish fat melted in a hollow stone, the string from your hoodie as a wick. A lamp. Steady, warm, and yours.
From here, the problems get smaller. But they keep coming.
Day thirteen: it rains somewhere above you, and the stream rises a meter in an hour. Your lamp drowns. Your fish are gone. One whole day back in the dark, rebuilding everything on a higher shelf.
Day fourteen: you crawl into a new tunnel, and your flame shrinks to a tiny blue dot. Bad air. Carbon dioxide pools in low spots, and miners used flames as an alarm. You back out. Slowly.
Day fifteen: you build a toilet. Downstream. Far downstream.
Day sixteen: you brush your teeth with charcoal and a finger, and finally take a bath. In ten-degree water. The scream echoes for a full minute.
Day seventeen: a rock the size of a TV falls from the ceiling exactly where you were sitting a second ago.
And day eighteen: you make a friend. An olm. A blind pink salamander that can live a hundred years and go ten without eating. People once thought they were baby dragons.
Steve. Your name is Steve.
And then something strange happens. You stop surviving. And start living.
You paint the walls with charcoal and clay, like people did forty thousand years ago. A sun. Your old apartment. Steve.
A table from a flat stone. A shelf. A bed of dry roots that's honestly better than your old mattress.
You move the glowing mushrooms onto the ceiling of your bedroom. Now you have stars.
The last real problem: your lamps burn fish oil faster than you can catch fish. So you weave a trap from roots and leave it in the stream. Now dinner catches itself.
You cook fish soup by dropping hot stones into water. You tap the stalactites and find out every one plays a different note.
There are twenty-four marks on your wall. And for the first time in your life, nobody needs anything from you.
Night, Steve.
Then, one morning, or maybe one night, the bell rings. From above.
Thirty days. Nobody has ever made it past day nine.
Thirty? I've only counted twenty-four.
Time runs slower down here. Everyone loses count. Your million.
A million dollars. A whole world up there. You look at the case. Then at your table. Your stars. Steve.
Can I... stay one more week?
Would you last thirty days down there? And what's the first thing you'd build? Tell me in the comments.
